name: Bonnor's Rotating Dust Cloud
description: A stationary, axially symmetric cloud of dust in rigid rotation that thins out to nothing in every direction, found by William Bonnor in 1977. Its total mass is zero, its centre is a singularity of negative mass, and the circles about the axis inside a torus around the centre are closed timelike curves.
convention: The length $a$ sets the rotation, with $a^2 = 2h$ for Bonnor's parameter $h$ and angular momentum $J = c^3a^2/2G$. We keep factors of $c$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Set a cloud of dust spinning and each grain can hold itself up on its own orbit, with no pressure anywhere [collas2004geodesics]. Can such a cloud be an island, thinning out to nothing in every direction? In Newton's gravity it cannot: dust that turns rigidly keeps one density all along its axis of rotation, so it is a cylinder with no top and no bottom [dearaujo2000]. That cylinder is a solution of general relativity too, found by Kornel Lanczos in 1924 and again by Willem Jacob van Stockum in 1937 [lanczos1924, vanstockum1937]. Van Stockum found more besides: every axially symmetric cloud of rigidly rotating dust follows from one solution of Laplace's equation, exactly as an electrostatic field does [vanstockum1937, ilyas2017].¶Take the simplest solution there is, the potential $2h/r$ of a point, and you get the cloud that William Bonnor, professor of mathematics at Queen Elizabeth College in London, published in 1977 [ilyas2017, maccallum2015, bonnor1977cloud]. The density of his dust is positive everywhere and dies away as the sixth power of the distance, so that the cloud, in his words, extends "tenuously to infinity" [bonnor1977cloud, collas2004frame]. The density also changes along the axis of rotation, and Bonnor explained why general relativity allows what Newton's gravity forbids [bonnor1977cloud, dearaujo2000]. Seen from far away, the cloud is a spinning body with angular momentum $J = c^3h/G$ and no mass [bratek2007, ilyas2017].¶No mass, in a cloud whose every grain has weight? The dust outside any sphere about the centre has a finite mass, and that mass grows without limit as the sphere shrinks [ilyas2017]. Bonnor's answer was that the centre, where his solution is singular, holds an infinite negative mass that cancels the infinite positive mass of the dust [dearaujo2000, astesiano2024]. The singularity has a direction to it as well: come in along the axis and the density and the curvature blow up, come in along the equatorial plane and both die away [astesiano2024]. Thirty years on, in Kraków, Łukasz Bratek, Joanna Jałocha, and Marek Kutschera proved the same of the whole class: any cloud of van Stockum's kind that is flat far away has zero total mass and singularities of negative mass [bratek2007].¶Circles misbehave near the centre: far out a circle around the axis is an ordinary circle, but inside a torus that hugs the singularity it is a closed timelike curve, a path a rocket could ride back to the event it started from [collas2004frame, astesiano2024]. At the Open University in 1999, B. R. Steadman followed light through the cloud and found a central region that no ray from infinity can enter and no ray from inside can leave, though the spacetime has no event horizon [steadman1999]. Peter Collas and David Klein, at California State University, Northridge, found a region near the centre where coordinate time runs backward along every freely falling path, and found paths that reach it from the flat region far away [collas2004geodesics]. They also noticed that the cloud drags a particle dropped with no angular momentum around the axis against the dust's own rotation [collas2004frame].¶Astronomers met the class in 2005, when Fred Cooperstock and S. Tieu modelled a spiral galaxy as rotating dust, following Bonnor's treatment, and argued that its rotation curve follows from the visible matter alone, with no halo of dark matter [cooperstock2005]. Tobias Zingg, Andreas Aste, and Dirk Trautmann, in Basel, examined such models and concluded that rotating dust cannot fill all of space as a galaxy model without turning unphysical somewhere [zingg2007]. Twelve years after Cooperstock and Tieu, Batyr Ilyas, Jinye Yang, Daniele Malafarina, and Cosimo Bambi put Bonnor's cloud itself to work, as a cloud of dark matter at the heart of a galaxy standing in for the supermassive black hole [ilyas2017]. They computed the light of a disc of gas orbiting inside it and found that the shape of its iron line could tell the cloud from a Kerr black hole, though perhaps not with the telescopes then flying [ilyas2017].¶Bonnor came away from his cloud wondering whether rotating dust can do without a singularity [dearaujo2000]. One answer trades the point for a sheet: José de Araujo and Anzhong Wang's cloud of 2000 is accompanied by a thin rotating disc of matter [dearaujo2000], and Bonnor's own second cloud, published in 2005 as "A rotating dust cloud in general relativity II", carries its negative mass as a layer spread over a plane [bonnor2005cloud, bratek2007]. The original cloud still draws visitors: in 2024 Davide Astesiano, Donato Bini, Andrea Geralico, and Matteo Luca Ruggiero sent test particles through its equatorial plane and found that those with angular momentum of one sign are turned back at the edge of the torus and never reach the singularity, while some with the other sign get in [astesiano2024].

related.text: Lanczos and van Stockum's cylinder belongs to the same class of rigidly rotating dust, with a twist that grows as the square of the distance from the axis where Bonnor's is a dipole's. The cylinder runs on along its axis without end, and Bonnor's cloud thins out in every direction [vanstockum1937, bratek2007].
The cloud with its rotation switched off, $a = 0$, where the density vanishes and the line element is flat space in cylindrical coordinates [astesiano2024].

Kurt Gödel's universe of 1949, rigidly rotating dust with a cosmological constant and one density everywhere. Its closed timelike curves pass through every event, and Bonnor's cloud keeps its own inside a torus about the centre [godel1949, astesiano2024].
Far from its centre Bonnor's cloud has the frame dragging term of Kerr's metric, for an angular momentum $J = c^3a^2/2G$, and no mass term to go with it [bratek2007].

A static vacuum field built on the potential of a point, as Bonnor's cloud is in van Stockum's class. Each has a singularity at the origin whose strength depends on the direction of approach [gautreau1967, ilyas2017, astesiano2024].

Dust in differential rotation filling all of space about an axis, regular everywhere. Bonnor and B. R. Steadman fitted a vacuum around a cylinder of it in 2009 and found no closed timelike curves inside or out [maitra1966, bonnor2009maitra].

coordinates.name: Cylindrical
domains: r^3 = a^2\rho \;\text{(the circles of constant } t, \rho, z \text{ are null)}
r^3 < a^2\rho \;\text{(the circles of constant } t, \rho, z \text{ are closed timelike curves)}

parameters.description: Rotation length, $a^2 = 2h = 2GJ/c^3$ with $h$ Bonnor's rotation parameter and $J$ the angular momentum at spatial infinity; the circle of constant $t$ in the equatorial plane is null at a distance $a$ from the centre
Distance from the centre in the flat space of the coordinates; the twist of the dust is $a^2\rho^2/r^3$, a dipole's, and its density is $c^2/8\pi G$ times the Ricci scalar

coordinates.convention: We use the comoving cylindrical coordinates $(t, \rho, \phi, z)$ of van Stockum's class, in which the dust is at rest, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, in the letters of Bratek, Jałocha, and Kutschera: Bonnor writes $r$ for our $\rho$ and $R$ for our $r = \sqrt{\rho^2 + z^2}$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Spherical
domains: r^2 = a^2\sin\theta \;\text{(the circles of constant } t, r, \theta \text{ are null)}
r^2 < a^2\sin\theta \;\text{(the circles of constant } t, r, \theta \text{ are closed timelike curves)}

parameters.description: Rotation length, $a^2 = 2h = 2GJ/c^3$ with $h$ Bonnor's rotation parameter and $J$ the angular momentum at spatial infinity; the circle of constant $t$ in the equatorial plane is null at a distance $a$ from the centre; the density of the dust is $c^2/8\pi G$ times the Ricci scalar

coordinates.convention: We use the spherical coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ of Bratek, Jałocha, and Kutschera, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, in which the dust is at rest and the cylindrical chart's $\rho = r\sin\theta$ and $z = r\cos\theta$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
